items.text: After the matching case runs, the switch ends even without break.
Without break, statements in switch blocks fall through into the following cases.
Selection statement: `switch (expr) { case v1: ...; break; ... default: ... }` chooses among many alternatives by the value of one expression.

The selector is an int-like (char, byte, short, int), String or enum expression. Case labels are distinct constants of that type, and default is optional. Control jumps to the matching label (or to default, or past the switch), and the case statements usually end with break. Without a break, execution falls through into the statements of the next case; default runs when no case matches.

Order: evaluate the selector once; compare it with the case constants; jump to the matching label (else default, else skip the switch). Then execute the statements from there in order, through later labels, until a break or the closing brace.
A switch statement has no value. Its result is the effect of the case(s) run: with `day = 3`, the S&W day switch prints Wed. Without breaks, day = 5 would print Fri, then Sat.
One execution evaluates the selector once (any side effect in it happens once) and runs the statements of one entry point and any cases it falls into. It changes only what those statements change.
A switch replaces an if-else chain only when every test is `expr == constant` on the same expression. Range tests such as the income-bracket chain (`income < 47450`) must stay an if-else chain.
Each case is normally ended by break, which exits the switch body. Leaving it out makes that case fall into the next. Inside a loop, that break exits the switch, not the loop.

Plan: multiway dispatch or lookup. It maps one discrete value (day number, menu choice, character) to one of several actions or results. Grouped labels (`case "apple": case "banana":`) map several values to one action.

When every case ends with break, reordering the cases does not change behaviour (labels are distinct constants). Removing one break changes behaviour for that value only. Adding a default changes only values with no matching label.

Use switch for more than two mutually exclusive alternatives decided by equality of one int, char, String or enum value. Use an if-else chain for ranges, doubles or unrelated conditions. Use an array lookup (S&W 1.4) when each case only selects a value.

Nested loops are a loop inside the body of another loop: the outer loop and the inner loop.
Because loops are statements, one can be the body of another; the inner loop iterates all the way through for each iteration of the outer loop.

Outer init; outer test; [inner init; inner test; inner body; inner update; ... until the inner test fails]; rest of the outer body; outer update; outer test; ... The inner init runs again on every outer pass.
The inner body runs (outer passes) x (inner passes) times: two loops of 1..10 call printf 100 times; DivisorPattern 3 prints 3 rows of 3 entries, each row ending with its row number.
One outer pass resets the inner variable, runs the complete inner loop, executes the rest of the outer body once, and then updates the outer variable once.
Usually both loops are for loops: the inner for runs its complete set of passes for every single pass of the outer for.
Matrix addition uses two nested loops over i and j; matrix multiplication adds a third, innermost loop over k for each dot product.
A plain break ends only the innermost loop; a labeled break is needed when the inner loop must end the outer one too.
Which loop is outside decides the visiting order: row index outside gives row-major order, column index outside gives column-major order.
Plan: process every pair (i, j) - two-dimensional tables, every row x column of a matrix, every pair of elements; the outer variable is a slow stepper, the inner a fast stepper.

items.text: Remainder operator %: the binary operator that gives the remainder after dividing a by b.
For ints, a % b is defined so that (a / b) * b + a % b equals a. The result takes the sign of a, % by zero throws ArithmeticException, and % also works on doubles.
Evaluate a, then b, take the quotient rounded toward 0, and give what is left over. % has the same precedence as * and /, and they group left to right.
r = a % b stores a remainder smaller in size than b and leaves a and b unchanged. If b is 0, ArithmeticException is thrown before anything is stored.
% is the companion of integer division, since a == (a / b) * b + a % b. Both use the same quotient rounded toward 0.
Plans: divisibility and parity tests (x % 2 == 0), digit extraction (x % 10), cyclic wrap-around ((i + 1) % n), leap-year rules, and splitting units (76 % 12 inches).

Negating a flips the remainder's sign, so n % 2 == 1 fails for negative odd n while n % 2 != 0 still works. Changing the divisor changes the cycle length. Swapping % with / swaps the remainder for the quotient.

Use % for divisibility, parity, digits, cyclic indices and unit splitting. Do not use it for percentages (use * / 100.0), and do not use it where a non-negative mathematical mod is needed for negative values (adjust the result or use Math.floorMod).

Selection statement: `switch (expr) { case v1: ...; break; ... default: ... }` chooses among many alternatives by the value of one expression.

The selector is an int-like (char, byte, short, int), String or enum expression. Case labels are distinct constants of that type, and default is optional. Control jumps to the matching label (or to default, or past the switch), and the case statements usually end with break. Without a break, execution falls through into the statements of the next case; default runs when no case matches.

Order: evaluate the selector once; compare it with the case constants; jump to the matching label (else default, else skip the switch). Then execute the statements from there in order, through later labels, until a break or the closing brace.
A switch statement has no value. Its result is the effect of the case(s) run: with `day = 3`, the S&W day switch prints Wed. Without breaks, day = 5 would print Fri, then Sat.
One execution evaluates the selector once (any side effect in it happens once) and runs the statements of one entry point and any cases it falls into. It changes only what those statements change.

Each case is normally ended by break, which exits the switch body. Leaving it out makes that case fall into the next. Inside a loop, that break exits the switch, not the loop.

Plan: multiway dispatch or lookup. It maps one discrete value (day number, menu choice, character) to one of several actions or results. Grouped labels (`case "apple": case "banana":`) map several values to one action.

When every case ends with break, reordering the cases does not change behaviour (labels are distinct constants). Removing one break changes behaviour for that value only. Adding a default changes only values with no matching label.

Use switch for more than two mutually exclusive alternatives decided by equality of one int, char, String or enum value. Use an if-else chain for ranges, doubles or unrelated conditions. Use an array lookup (S&W 1.4) when each case only selects a value.
